title: Beneficial Shares in the Family Home
subtitle: From Rosset to Kernott: how the courts learned to read a relationship
objectives: Explain the common intention constructive trust and why it is used to determine beneficial ownership of the family home separately from legal title
Distinguish the sole-name analysis in Lloyds Bank v Rosset from the joint-names analysis in Stack v Dowden and Jones v Kernott, and identify which applies on given facts
Apply the principles for quantifying beneficial shares, including the court's power to impute a common intention that neither party actually held

leadingAuthorities.role: Sole-name cases: a share arises only from an express agreement plus detrimental reliance, or a direct financial contribution to acquisition
Joint-names cases: a presumption of equal beneficial ownership, displaceable by the parties' whole course of dealing
Confirms Stack, and permits the court to impute a fair share where intention changed but cannot be precisely inferred from the evidence
The Stack approach is not confined to domestic cohabiting couples, but a commercial purpose is powerful evidence pointing back towards resulting-trust-style shares

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is one of the few topics on the course that maps directly onto real heartbreak — who gets what share of the house when a relationship ends. Where the profile shows knowledge outpacing application, this note appears: 'You can recite Rosset, Stack and Kernott — this lesson is about knowing which one a given couple's facts actually call for.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the case names well. The test pool below leans hard on application — expect fact patterns where you have to work out whether a couple is in sole-name or joint-name territory before you can even pick the right test.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Take Parts 1 to 3 slowly and make sure you can state, without prompting, what changes between a sole-name case and a joint-names case — the later material assumes you already have that distinction cold.

overview.hook: The house is in his name only. For nine years she has paid the council tax, decorated every room, and raised their children in it — but never once paid towards the mortgage. When they split up, does she own any of it at all? Thirty years ago, English law's answer was close to no. This lesson is the story of how, and how far, that answer changed.

parts.heading: One name on the title, two people's lives in the house
parts.voice: narrative — the human stakes are set out before any doctrine is named, because the doctrine only makes sense once the stakes are clear
body: Legal title to a house tells you whose name is on the Land Registry entry. It does not, on its own, tell you who owns the house in the eyes of equity. Those two things can and often do diverge — most sharply when a couple's relationship ends and only one of them was ever named as legal owner.

The device equity uses to close that gap is the common intention constructive trust: a trust the court finds existed, informally and often unspoken, because the parties' words or conduct show they intended the property to be shared beneficially, even though only one of them holds the legal title.

For decades, the leading case setting the test for sole-name cases was Lloyds Bank v Rosset. Mrs Rosset had put a great deal of unpaid labour into renovating a derelict farmhouse bought in her husband's sole name — decorating, supervising builders, doing manual work herself — but had not contributed a penny to the purchase price. When the bank later sought to repossess the house over her husband's debts, she argued she had a beneficial share that gave her the right to remain.

The House of Lords set out a strict, two-track test for sole-name cases. A non-owner can establish a share only by showing either: (1) an express agreement, arrangement or understanding between the parties that the property would be shared — however informally reached, even a vague conversation counts — together with the non-owner acting to their detriment in reliance on it; or (2) a direct financial contribution to the purchase price, such as paying towards the deposit or the mortgage instalments. On Rosset's own facts, renovation work — however substantial, however genuinely believed by Mrs Rosset to be 'her' contribution to their home — satisfied neither limb, and she was held to have no beneficial interest at all.

components.definition: A trust equity imposes over property held in one party's sole legal name, recognising a beneficial share for another person where their words or conduct show a shared intention that the property be owned beneficially between them.

components.factsShort: Mrs Rosset did substantial unpaid renovation work on a house bought in her husband's sole name, but made no financial contribution to its purchase.
components.ratioShort: In a sole-name case, only an express agreement plus detrimental reliance, or a direct financial contribution to acquisition, can found a beneficial share — indirect contributions like unpaid labour are not enough.

expanded.facts: Mr Rosset bought a derelict farmhouse with money from a family trust, in his sole name, without his wife's knowledge or involvement in the purchase itself. Before completion, Mrs Rosset threw herself into renovating the property — decorating, organising builders, and doing manual work — in the expectation the family would live there together. Mr Rosset later took out a loan secured on the house without her knowledge, and defaulted. The bank sought possession; Mrs Rosset resisted, claiming a beneficial interest with a right to occupy that bound the bank.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Bridge held that, absent an express agreement supported by detrimental reliance, the court should not readily infer a common intention to share ownership from conduct alone — and that only direct contributions to the purchase price, referable to the acquisition of the property, would found an inferred common intention on the facts of a sole-name case. Renovation work, however substantial, fell on the wrong side of that line.
expanded.significance: Rosset set a famously strict, narrow test that many later judges (and the Law Commission) criticised as out of step with how ordinary couples actually organise their finances and their lives. It remains the starting point for sole-name cases, but its strictness is precisely what the later joint-names cases moved away from for co-owned property.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that unpaid renovation work alone, with no financial contribution to the purchase price, was enough to give Mrs Rosset a beneficial share under the strict test in Lloyds Bank v Rosset?
interaction.explanation: Rosset drew the line sharply: absent an express agreement with detrimental reliance, only direct financial contributions to the purchase price would do. Renovation work, however substantial and however genuinely relied upon by Mrs Rosset, was held not to satisfy either limb of the test.

parts.heading: Joint names change the starting point
parts.voice: doctrinal — traces the reasoning in Stack v Dowden closely, treating the shift in method as the real story
body: Rosset's strict test was developed for sole-name cases, where equity has to find a share for someone with no title at all. Where a couple's names are both on the legal title, the House of Lords held in Stack v Dowden that a different starting point applies entirely.

Ms Dowden and Mr Stack had lived together for eighteen years and had four children, but kept their finances scrupulously separate throughout the relationship — separate bank accounts, separate savings, and a pattern of Ms Dowden paying substantially more than Mr Stack towards the house, which was registered in both their names. When they separated, Mr Stack argued for an equal, 50/50 split; Ms Dowden argued her share should reflect her far larger financial contribution.

The House of Lords held that where legal title is held jointly, equity starts from the presumption that beneficial ownership is also held jointly and equally — 'equity follows the law.' That starting presumption reflects the reality that most couples who put a house in joint names intend to share it equally, and does not require anyone to prove anything to get there.

But the presumption is not fixed. It can be displaced by evidence about the parties' whole course of dealing in relation to the property — not merely who paid what towards the purchase price, but how they organised their finances more generally, why the property was put into joint names, and how they arranged their lives around the home over time. On Stack's own unusual facts — the rigorously separate finances throughout — the presumption of equality was displaced, and Ms Dowden was awarded 65% of the property.

The deeper significance of Stack is a shift in method as much as outcome: instead of narrowing the inquiry to financial contributions, the House of Lords opened it up into a genuinely holistic look at how a particular couple actually lived with their property.

components.factsShort: A long-term couple held their home in joint names but kept finances rigorously separate; Ms Dowden had contributed far more towards the property.
components.ratioShort: Joint legal title starts with a presumption of equal beneficial ownership, displaceable by evidence of the parties' whole course of dealing in relation to the property.

expanded.facts: Ms Dowden and Mr Stack were unmarried and lived together for eighteen years, raising four children, but never pooled their finances — each kept separate bank accounts and financial affairs throughout. The family home was registered in their joint names, with Ms Dowden having paid considerably more towards its purchase and outgoings than Mr Stack.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The majority held that in joint-names cases the starting point is a presumption of equal beneficial ownership, reflecting the equitable maxim that equity follows the law. That presumption yields, however, to evidence — assessed by reference to the parties' whole course of dealing, not confined to financial contributions to the purchase price — that they intended their beneficial shares to differ. On these unusual facts, the presumption was displaced and shares of 65% (Ms Dowden) and 35% (Mr Stack) were found.
expanded.significance: Stack fixed the presumption of equality as the joint-names starting point and, more importantly, broadened the evidence a court can consider when that presumption is challenged — a genuinely holistic inquiry into how the couple lived, not a narrow accounting exercise.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Stack v Dowden, highlight the sentence that states the governing presumption for joint-names cases.
interaction.passage: Where a family home is conveyed into joint names, equity follows the law, and the starting point is that the parties are entitled to the beneficial interest in equal shares. That presumption can only be displaced by evidence of a different common intention, to be gathered from the whole course of dealing between the parties in relation to the property, not confined to their respective financial contributions.
interaction.ratioSentence: Where a family home is conveyed into joint names, equity follows the law, and the starting point is that the parties are entitled to the beneficial interest in equal shares.

parts.heading: Kernott: when the couple never agreed, but time did the talking
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the hard problem Stack left unresolved before showing how the Supreme Court answered it
body: Stack tells a court to look at the whole course of dealing and infer what the parties actually intended. But what should a court do when the honest answer is that the parties never turned their minds to the question at all — when there is genuinely no evidence of what they thought their shares should be, only evidence of how they lived?

That was the problem in Jones v Kernott. Ms Jones and Mr Kernott bought a house in joint names as an unmarried couple. Their relationship ended after eight years; Mr Kernott moved out, and for the following fourteen years made no further contribution at all — no mortgage payments, no maintenance, nothing towards the children's upkeep — while Ms Jones paid everything and raised their children in the house alone. When the house was eventually sold, should the proceeds still be split 50/50, simply because that was the position at the point of purchase?

The Supreme Court confirmed Stack's starting presumption of equality in joint-names cases, but went one step further. Where the evidence shows that the parties' common intention as to their respective shares changed at some point after acquisition, but the court cannot work out precisely what new percentages they actually intended, the court may impute a fair share to each of them — not infer what they actually thought, but attribute to them whatever share the court considers fair, judged against the whole course of dealing.

That distinction between inferring and imputing is the real intellectual move in Kernott. Inferring intention still asks a factual question: what did these two people actually think, on the evidence available? Imputing intention asks something different: what would be fair, given how they in fact lived, once the court is satisfied there is no honest answer to the first question at all. On the facts, the Supreme Court upheld a 90/10 split in Ms Jones's favour, reflecting her sole financial and practical responsibility for the mortgage, the household and the children for fourteen years after separation.

components.label: Infer vs impute — the Kernott distinction
points: Inferring intention: a finding of fact — what the parties actually intended, based on evidence of what they said or did
Imputing intention: attributing to the parties whatever share the court considers fair, used only once the court is satisfied that actual intention genuinely cannot be inferred from the evidence
Imputation is not available in sole-name cases in the same way — Rosset's stricter test still governs whether a share exists at all before any question of quantification arises

interaction.prompt: Leo and Maya buy a house in joint names as an unmarried couple. After four years, Leo moves out and never contributes to the mortgage, bills or upkeep again. Maya pays everything for the next eleven years, and the couple never discuss what their shares should be. The house is later sold. Analyse how the proceeds should be divided.
factsToOrder: Leo and Maya hold the house in joint names
Leo moves out after four years and stops contributing entirely
Maya pays everything for the following eleven years
The parties never discuss or agree what their shares should be

modelAnswer.issue: Whether, and in what shares, Leo and Maya are beneficially entitled to the proceeds of sale.
modelAnswer.rule: Joint legal title starts with a presumption of equal beneficial shares (Stack v Dowden). That presumption can be displaced by the parties' whole course of dealing. Where the evidence shows their common intention as to shares changed after acquisition but the court cannot precisely infer the new percentages, the court may impute a fair share to each (Jones v Kernott).
modelAnswer.application: Leo's total withdrawal from financial and practical responsibility after four years, set against Maya's eleven years of sole responsibility, is strong evidence that the parties' intentions changed from the initial equal split. But since they never discussed or agreed new shares, the court cannot simply infer a precise new percentage from express words — it must impute a fair share, looking at the whole course of dealing, much as in Kernott itself.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The starting presumption of equal shares is displaced by the parties' course of dealing after separation; applying Kernott, a court is likely to impute shares heavily favouring Maya, reflecting her sole responsibility for the property over the following eleven years.

parts.heading: Beyond the family home: Marr v Collie
parts.voice: comparative — tests whether the doctrine is really about romance, or about something the courts can apply more broadly
body: Every case so far has involved a cohabiting couple and a home they lived in together. Marr v Collie asks a sharper question: is the Stack approach — holistic, focused on the whole course of dealing — a special rule for domestic relationships, or a general method that applies to any joint legal owners, wherever it's appropriate?

The parties in Marr v Collie were former civil partners who had also been business partners, and who together bought several properties in the Bahamas — some used as family homes, others let out or held for investment — registering some, but not all, in joint names. When the relationship ended, the question was which method of analysis applied to which property: the Stack-style holistic inquiry, or a more traditional resulting trust approach based straightforwardly on who paid what.

The Privy Council held that Stack's holistic approach is not confined to a purely 'domestic consumer context' — it can, in principle, apply to any joint legal owners, wherever the facts warrant asking what their whole relationship shows about their common intention. But the Board was equally clear that context still matters enormously: where a property was acquired for a primarily commercial or investment purpose, that purpose is itself powerful evidence pointing back towards resulting-trust-style reasoning — shares proportionate to financial contribution — rather than an assumed equality that makes far more sense for a shared family home.

The lesson is not that Rosset and Stack/Kernott have been replaced by one universal rule. It's that the choice of method is itself a judgment about the nature of the relationship and the purpose of the purchase — and a student who can explain why a test applies, not just which test applies, is answering the question examiners are actually asking.

components.factsShort: Former civil and business partners jointly acquired several Bahamian properties, some domestic and some investment; the Board had to decide which analytical approach applied.
components.ratioShort: The Stack holistic approach is not limited to domestic cohabitation, but a commercial or investment purpose is strong evidence favouring resulting-trust-style, contribution-based shares instead.

expanded.facts: Mr Marr and Mr Collie were former civil partners who had also run a business together. Over the course of their relationship they acquired several properties in the Bahamas, some intended as homes and others as investments, financed in varying and sometimes commercially-structured ways, and registered in a mix of sole and joint names. After separation, a dispute arose over the correct method for determining beneficial ownership of the jointly-held properties.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Board held that the reasoning in Stack v Dowden was not, as a matter of principle, confined to the domestic consumer context in which it arose; the touchstone is always what the parties' common intention was, assessed by reference to their whole relevant course of dealing. However, where the purpose and structure of a joint acquisition is essentially commercial, that context will often itself be the clearest evidence pointing away from a presumption of equality and back towards shares reflecting financial contribution, consistently with resulting trust principles.
expanded.significance: Marr v Collie confirms that Stack's method is a general one, not a rule reserved for romantic cohabitation — but it also confirms that context, including commercial purpose, remains central to deciding which set of presumptions actually fits the facts.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario points most strongly towards resulting-trust-style, contribution-based shares rather than Stack's presumption of equality?
interaction.scenarioA: A cohabiting couple buy their only home in joint names, live in it together for years, and raise children there.
interaction.scenarioB: Two business partners jointly buy a rental property purely as an investment, each contributing a different, carefully documented amount towards the price, with no intention of ever living there.
interaction.explanation: As Marr v Collie confirms, a purchase that is essentially commercial in purpose — an investment property bought by business partners with carefully tracked, unequal contributions — is itself powerful evidence favouring shares proportionate to contribution, rather than the presumption of equality that fits a couple's shared family home in scenario A.

parts.heading: Bringing it together: which test, which question
parts.voice: direct — a working method for exam answers, closing the narrative arc that opened this lesson
body: Four cases, one underlying question: who owns the beneficial interest in property one or more people live in, or invest in, together? The route through them is a sequence of questions, not a single test.

First: is the legal title in one name or joint names? Sole name sends you to Rosset — a share can only be established by an express agreement with detrimental reliance, or a direct financial contribution to acquisition. No share, no further questions about quantification.
Second, in joint names: start from Stack's presumption of equal beneficial shares. Ask whether the whole course of dealing — not just financial contributions — displaces that presumption.

Third: if the presumption is displaced, or if it's clear the parties' intentions genuinely changed over time, try to infer what shares they actually intended from the evidence. Only if that fails — if there's truly no honest inference available — does Jones v Kernott let the court impute a fair share instead.

Fourth, always check context: Marr v Collie is the reminder that this whole framework assumes a relationship and a purpose that justify it. A commercial or investment purchase may call for straightforward resulting-trust reasoning even between joint legal owners, whatever the state of their personal relationship.

components.title: Beneficial shares: the decision path
components.description: The sequence of questions a court works through to determine beneficial ownership of jointly used or jointly owned property.

nodes.label: Is legal title held in one name or joint names?
Sole name → apply Rosset: express agreement + detriment, or direct financial contribution to acquisition. No share found on either limb → no beneficial interest at all.
Joint names → start from Stack's presumption of equal beneficial shares
Does the whole course of dealing displace the presumption of equality?
Can the actual intended shares be inferred from the evidence?
If not, and intention has genuinely changed, the court may impute a fair share (Kernott)
Check purpose throughout: a commercial/investment context may favour resulting-trust, contribution-based shares instead (Marr v Collie)

components.textAlternative: First ask whether legal title is in one name or joint names. In a sole name case, apply Rosset: a share requires either an express agreement with detrimental reliance, or a direct financial contribution to acquisition; without either, there is no beneficial interest. In a joint names case, start from Stack's presumption of equal shares, then ask whether the parties' whole course of dealing displaces it. If it does, try to infer the shares the parties actually intended; only if that is genuinely impossible does Kernott allow the court to impute a fair share instead. Throughout, check the purpose of the purchase — a commercial or investment context, per Marr v Collie, may point back towards resulting-trust, contribution-based shares regardless of joint legal title.

interaction.prompt: Put these questions in the order a court works through them when determining beneficial shares in jointly-owned property.
items: Is legal title held in one name or joint names?
If joint names, does the presumption of equal shares apply as the starting point?
Does the whole course of dealing displace that presumption?
If displaced, can the actual intended shares be inferred, or must a fair share be imputed instead?
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the whole route: title first, then the joint-names presumption, then whether the course of dealing displaces it, and only then the infer/impute question from Kernott.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — you can't ask whether the presumption is displaced before establishing that you're in joint-names territory in the first place, and infer/impute only becomes relevant once displacement is established.

testPool.prompt: Name the doctrine used to find that someone not on the legal title nonetheless has a beneficial share in a property.
testPool.modelAnswer: The common intention constructive trust — a trust equity recognises where the parties' words or conduct show a shared intention that the property be beneficially owned between them, despite legal title being held by only one of them.

testPool.prompt: Under the strict Rosset test, is paying household bills and raising children, without any financial contribution to the purchase price, enough on its own to found a beneficial share in a sole-name case?
options: No — indirect contributions of that kind do not satisfy either limb of the Rosset test
Yes — any meaningful contribution to family life is treated as equivalent to a financial contribution

testPool.prompt: Which of the following would satisfy the Rosset test for a beneficial share in a sole-name case?
options: An express agreement to share ownership, plus detrimental reliance on it
Doing all the housework and childcare for the whole relationship, with no financial contribution
Being named as next of kin on the other party's insurance policy
testPool.trapExplanation: Housework and childcare, however substantial, are indirect contributions that Rosset does not treat as sufficient on their own; being named on an insurance policy says nothing about intentions regarding the property itself. Only an express agreement with detrimental reliance, or a direct financial contribution to acquisition, satisfies the test.

testPool.prompt: In a joint-names case, what is the starting presumption under Stack v Dowden?
options: Equal beneficial shares, displaceable by the whole course of dealing
Shares strictly proportionate to each party's financial contribution to the purchase price

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Jones v Kernott, highlight the sentence that states when a court may impute, rather than infer, a common intention.
testPool.passage: Where the evidence shows that the parties' common intention as to their respective shares has changed over time, but there is no evidence from which their actual, changed intentions can be inferred, the court is entitled to impute an intention which the parties never actually had, attributing to them the share the court considers fair having regard to the whole course of dealing between them.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where the evidence shows that the parties' common intention as to their respective shares has changed over time, but there is no evidence from which their actual, changed intentions can be inferred, the court is entitled to impute an intention which the parties never actually had, attributing to them the share the court considers fair having regard to the whole course of dealing between them.

testPool.prompt: Put these developments in the order they occurred.
items: Lloyds Bank v Rosset sets a strict test for sole-name cases
Stack v Dowden establishes a presumption of equal shares for joint-names cases
Jones v Kernott confirms the court can impute a fair share where intention cannot be inferred
Marr v Collie confirms the Stack approach is not confined to domestic cohabiting couples

testPool.prompt: What is the key difference between inferring and imputing a common intention as to beneficial shares?
options: Inferring is a finding about what the parties actually intended on the evidence; imputing is the court attributing a fair share once actual intention genuinely cannot be found
Inferring only applies to sole-name cases, and imputing only to joint-names cases
There is no real difference — the two words describe the same process
testPool.trapExplanation: Both processes can arise within joint-names cases; the distinction is not about which type of case they apply to, but about whether the court is finding a fact (inference) or substituting its own judgment of fairness once no fact can be found (imputation).

testPool.prompt: Does Marr v Collie hold that Stack's holistic, whole-course-of-dealing approach can never apply outside a romantic cohabiting relationship?
options: No — it confirms the approach is not confined to the domestic context, though a commercial purpose is strong evidence for a different, contribution-based analysis
Yes — it confines Stack strictly to married or cohabiting couples living together

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that would count as a direct financial contribution to acquisition under the Rosset test.
testPool.scenarioText: The house is in Callum's sole name. His partner Rhea painted and wallpapered every room after they moved in, cooked every meal for years, and separately paid half of the original mortgage deposit directly to the solicitors handling the purchase.
tappableSpans: paid half of the original mortgage deposit directly to the solicitors
testPool.correctSpan: paid half of the original mortgage deposit directly to the solicitors
testPool.explanation: Painting and cooking are indirect, non-financial contributions that Rosset does not treat as sufficient. Paying towards the deposit, directly connected to the purchase itself, is precisely the kind of direct financial contribution that can found a beneficial share in a sole-name case.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario calls for the Rosset test, rather than the Stack/Kernott approach?
testPool.scenarioA: A house bought and registered in the sole name of one partner, with the other partner claiming a share despite having no name on the title.
testPool.scenarioB: A house bought and registered in the joint names of both partners, who dispute only how large each of their shares should be.
testPool.explanation: Rosset governs whether a non-titled party has any beneficial share at all in a sole-name case. Once title is joint, as in B, the question is never whether a share exists — both already have one — but how large it is, which is Stack and Kernott territory, not Rosset.

testPool.prompt: A couple buy a house in joint names. Throughout the relationship they pool all income into one account, pay all bills from it jointly, and have never discussed or documented individual shares. On separation, one argues for a 70/30 split reflecting a slightly higher salary. What is the likely starting point, and is it easily displaced on these facts?
options: The starting point is equal shares (Stack); pooled finances and no evidence of any different intention make this presumption very hard to displace
The starting point is shares proportionate to salary, because higher earnings always displace the presumption of equality
There is no presumption at all in joint-names cases; the court must calculate contributions from scratch every time
testPool.explanation: Stack starts joint-names cases at equal shares. Far from displacing that presumption, pooled finances and the absence of any evidence of a different shared intention are exactly the kind of course of dealing that reinforces it — a higher salary alone, without more, is not enough to displace equality.

testPool.prompt: Priya and Sam buy a house in joint names. After six years, Sam is made redundant and stops contributing to the mortgage, while Priya takes on full financial responsibility for the next nine years, also funding a major extension to the house from her own savings. They never discuss what this means for their shares. On sale, how should the proceeds likely be divided?
factsToOrder: Priya and Sam hold the house in joint names
Sam stops contributing to the mortgage after six years
Priya solely funds the mortgage and a major extension for the following nine years
The parties never discuss or agree new shares

modelAnswer.issue: Whether, and in what proportions, Priya and Sam are beneficially entitled to the sale proceeds.
modelAnswer.rule: Joint legal title starts from a presumption of equal shares (Stack v Dowden), displaceable by the whole course of dealing; where intention has changed but cannot be precisely inferred, the court may impute a fair share (Jones v Kernott).
modelAnswer.application: Sam's withdrawal from financial responsibility after six years, against Priya's nine years of sole funding including a substantial capital investment in the extension, is strong evidence the parties' intentions changed from an equal split. As they never discussed new shares, no precise figure can be inferred from express words, so a court is likely to impute a fair share reflecting Priya's markedly greater and more recent contribution, much as in Kernott itself.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The presumption of equality is displaced by the parties' subsequent course of dealing; applying Kernott, the court is likely to impute shares significantly favouring Priya, reflecting her sole responsibility and capital investment over the following nine years.

testPool.prompt: Two friends who are not in a romantic relationship jointly buy a flat purely to let it out for rental income, each contributing a carefully documented and unequal sum towards the price, with a written record of their respective contributions. Which analytical approach is most appropriate?
options: A resulting-trust-style approach with shares proportionate to contribution, since the purchase is commercial and the parties themselves documented their contributions
The Stack presumption of equal shares, because the property is jointly owned regardless of purpose
The Rosset test, because at least one party may not be on the legal title
testPool.explanation: As Marr v Collie confirms, a purely commercial or investment purpose — here reinforced by the parties' own documented, unequal contributions — is strong evidence pointing towards resulting-trust reasoning based on contribution, rather than Stack's presumption of equality, which fits a shared family home far better than an arm's-length investment.

testPool.prompt: A married couple buy their family home in joint names. Neither has ever discussed how it would be split if they separated. Does the court start by trying to work out each party's financial contribution before deciding their shares?
options: No — it starts from the presumption of equal shares under Stack, and only looks further if that presumption is challenged
Yes — contribution is always the first and primary question in every co-ownership case

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is applying Rosset's strict sole-name test to a joint-names case, or vice versa. The very first question is always whose name is on the legal title — get that wrong, and every later step of the analysis answers the wrong question.
